newsitem.title: USA: US rate hikes would slow growth in Q3-4 '97-Brusca.
newsitem.headline: US rate hikes would slow growth in Q3-4 '97-Brusca.

text.p: Federal Reserve interest rate hikes in the first half of the year would slow the U.S. economy in the second half of 1997, a Wall Street economist argued on Tuesday.
At a press briefing, Nikko International chief economist Robert Brusca said inflation will accelerate, along with growth, in the first part of 1997.
Later in 1997, the economy is likely to slow in response to rate hikes that will accumulate by midyear, he said.
Brusca said he believes the Fed will raise interest rates by 50 basis points before the end of the first quarter.
He said the 30-year Treasury bond yield would ease to 6.6 percent in the fourth quarter.
Brusca said monthly non-farm payroll growth of 160,000 was the "speed limit" for the economy with an unemployment rate at its current 5.3 percent.

"If you're seeing numbers much stronger than that, chances are you're seeing excessive wage pressures -- at least at this rate of employment -- and you start to get some worries about inflation in the economy," he said.
Brusca said narrower trade deficits accounted for the fourth quarter of 1996 being stronger than forecast.
He forecast first quarter Gross Domestic Product growth at 2.8 percent, second quarter growth at 3.3 percent, the third quarter at 1.9 percent and fourth quarter GDP at 1.6 percent.

Brusca said he did not expect the Fed to raise rates at its Feb 4-5 meeting, though he called that conclusion "a close call" that could change in the face of "bad news" like a strong rise in the fourth-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI).
The fourth-quarter ECI is due on January 28.
"The Fed will look at the ECI very closely," he said.
Brusca said the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond yield would rise to 7.4 percent in the second quarter.
"The big surprise in the fourth quarter was trade," said Brusca. "The trade numbers have shrunk to nothingness, giving a big boost to GDP (Gross Domestic Product)."

Brusca theorized that the trade gap shrunk in the fourth quarter because seasonal adjustments post too much export growth in the fourth quarter. He said he expects the U.S. trade gap to shrink in real terms this year.
"It's something that's going to happen; it just hasn't happened yet," he said.
Brusca said the Boskin Commission, the group that studied the Consumer Price Index (CPI) "could hurt" the CPI.
"CPI can either be a good relative gauge or a good absolute gauge, but not both," said Brusca.
About the current inflation outlook, Brusca said, "I'm not worried about a big inflation surge, but we have some creeping inflation."
Regarding the equity market, Brusca said, "Last year I liked the stock market. I don't hate the stock market now. I'm still forecasting good economic growth."
Brusca said there could be "some kind of setback" in the stock market at midyear, but said the market's direction is "really a matter of (corporate) earnings.
"These stock prices are supported by earnings growth and inflation has been lower," he said.
Brusca said the talk of investing some Social Security funds in stocks, adjusting the CPI and balancing the budget are all "stock market friendly" notions.
"Do you really want to sell stocks if they put Social Security money into equities?" asked Brusca rhetorically.
He said price-earnings ratios "are really about where they normally are in low-inflation periods."
But the stock market's performance now depends on the earnings side of the price-earnings ratio, he said.
